questions.stem: A patient presents with the constellation of findings depicted here (blind as a bat, dry as a bone, red as a beet, hot as a hare, mad as a hatter). Which agent is used to reverse this toxidrome?

explanation.summary: The illustration depicts the anticholinergic (antimuscarinic) toxidrome. Physostigmine, a centrally acting acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, raises synaptic acetylcholine to overcome muscarinic blockade and is the antidote. Atropine would worsen it, pralidoxime treats organophosphate poisoning, naloxone reverses opioids, and flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines.
explanation.whyCorrect: The illustration depicts the anticholinergic (antimuscarinic) toxidrome. Physostigmine, a centrally acting acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, raises synaptic acetylcholine to overcome muscarinic blockade and is the antidote. Atropine would worsen it, pralidoxime treats organophosphate poisoning, naloxone reverses opioids, and flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Atropine is a muscarinic antagonist that causes this toxidrome; giving it would worsen symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepine sedation and does not counter muscarinic blockade.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Naloxone reverses opioid toxicity, with miosis and respiratory depression, not anticholinergic signs.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pralidoxime regenerates acetylcholinesterase after organophosphate poisoning, the opposite (cholinergic) toxidrome.

questions.stem: Based on this illustration of a cholinergic synapse, how do the antagonist molecules shown at the target cell membrane produce their pharmacologic effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They block the release of acetylcholine from the synaptic vesicles

choices.label: B
choices.text: They competitively occupy the muscarinic receptors

choices.label: C
choices.text: They directly activate the receptors to mimic acetylcholine

choices.label: D
choices.text: They enzymatically degrade acetylcholine within the synaptic cleft

choices.label: E
choices.text: They prevent the nerve impulse from reaching the presynaptic terminal

explanation.summary: Anticholinergics are muscarinic antagonists that act by competitive inhibition, binding the receptor without activating it so that endogenous acetylcholine cannot exert its effect on the target cell.
explanation.whyCorrect: Anticholinergics are muscarinic antagonists that act by competitive inhibition, binding the receptor without activating it so that endogenous acetylcholine cannot exert its effect on the target cell.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Blocking vesicular acetylcholine release is how botulinum toxin works, acting presynaptically rather than at the target cell receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Directly activating receptors to mimic acetylcholine describes agonists like bethanechol or pilocarpine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Degrading acetylcholine in the cleft is the job of acetylcholinesterase, not a receptor antagonist.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Preventing nerve impulse propagation describes local anesthetics or sodium channel blockers acting on the axon.

questions.stem: The schematic contrasts the normal action of the labeled mediator on its receptor (left) with drug therapy that occupies the same receptor (right). To which receptor superfamily does the receptor depicted in this diagram belong?

explanation.summary: The diagram depicts the H1 histamine receptor, a seven-transmembrane G protein-coupled receptor. Histamine released from the activated mast cell binds this GPCR to trigger downstream effects (itching, swelling, inflammation); an H1 antagonist occupies the receptor and leaves it inactive, preventing signaling. H1 receptors are not ion channels, kinase receptors, or nuclear receptors.
explanation.whyCorrect: The diagram depicts the H1 histamine receptor, a seven-transmembrane G protein-coupled receptor. Histamine released from the activated mast cell binds this GPCR to trigger downstream effects (itching, swelling, inflammation); an H1 antagonist occupies the receptor and leaves it inactive, preventing signaling. H1 receptors are not ion channels, kinase receptors, or nuclear receptors.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Receptor tyrosine kinases, such as insulin and growth factor receptors, have intrinsic enzymatic activity, unlike H1 receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ligand-gated ion channels open a pore directly, as with nicotinic or 5-HT3 receptors; H1 signals through Gq.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nuclear hormone receptors are intracellular and bind lipophilic ligands like steroids, not histamine at the cell surface.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Guanylyl cyclase-linked receptors bind natriuretic peptides and generate cGMP, which is not how histamine acts at H1.
